# 🚀 Mini Project — Deploying an NGINX Server in AWS Using Terraform

Focus: AWS + Terraform + Ubuntu + NGINX + Infrastructure as Code

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-12.png" /></p>

## 📌 Project Overview

This mini project demonstrates how to provision an AWS environment with Terraform, launch an Ubuntu EC2 instance, and configure an NGINX web server automatically.

The project covers:

- Creating an AWS VPC

- Configuring public/private subnets

- Creating an Internet Gateway and Route Table

- Associating subnets with the Route Table

- Launching an Ubuntu EC2 instance

- Configuring an AWS Security Group

- Creating and using an EC2 Key Pair

Using Terraform user_data for server initialization

- Installing and starting NGINX automatically

Understanding Terraform lifecycle behavior

- Troubleshooting Terraform and startup-script issues

The original project notes also document several implementation problems and their resolutions, making this project useful as both a deployment example and a troubleshooting/learning reference.

## 🎯 Objective

Build a repeatable AWS infrastructure deployment in which Terraform provisions the required networking and compute resources, while an EC2 startup script installs and configures NGINX.

### Expected Outcome

Terraform

│

├ ── VPC

├ ── Public / Private Subnets

├ ── Internet Gateway

├ ── Route Table

├ ── Security Group

├ ── Key Pair (can be omitted)

│

└── Ubuntu EC2 Instance

│

└── user_data

│

├ ── apt-get update

├ ── install NGINX

├ ── enable NGINX

└── start NGINX

## 📁 Terraform Files

The project notes describe three Terraform files:

### `ngnix_instanceConfig.tf`

Contains configuration related to the AWS Ubuntu instance, including:

- EC2 instance configuration

- user_data

- Key Pair (can be omitted)

### `ngnix_networkConfig.tf`

Contains AWS networking resources, including:

- VPC

- Subnets

- Internet Gateway

- Route Table

### `ngnix_tfConfig.tf`

Contains:

- Terraform providers

- Provider versions

- AWS region configuration

## ⚙️ Deployment Flow

A typical deployment flow for this project is:

1. Configure Terraform provider

↓

2. Create VPC

↓

3. Create subnets

↓

4. Create Internet Gateway

↓

5. Create Route Table

↓

6. Associate subnet(s)

↓

7. Create Security Group

↓

8. Create EC2 Key Pair

↓

9. Launch Ubuntu EC2 instance

↓

10. Execute user_data

↓

11. Install & configure NGINX

↓

12. Access the server

# 🧪 Challenges & Troubleshooting

A key purpose of this project was learning from deployment failures rather than only documenting the final working configuration.

## Error 1: Terraform- ROUTE TABLE ASSOCIATION Failure

### Problem

The

explicit subnet association within the Route Table was not attaching as expected, even after attempting a manual association.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-10.png" /></p>

### Diagnosis

The project notes identified inconsistent resource naming between the Route Table and Route Table Association.

### Resolution

The resource names were aligned consistently.

The working configuration concept was:

```hcl
## Route Table resource " aws_route_table " " my_rtb " { vpc _id = aws_vpc.my_vpc.id route { cidr _block = "0.0.0.0/0" gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.my_igw.id } tags = merge( local.tags , { Name = " routeTable " } ) # lifecycle { # create_before_destroy = true # } }
```

## Route Table Association resource " aws_route_table_association " " rtb_associate " { route _table_id = aws_route_table.my_rtb.id subnet_id = aws_subnet.my_subnet.id lifecycle { create _before_destroy = true } }

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-5.png" /></p>

### Result

The subnet association worked and outbound traffic between the instance/network and Internet Gateway worked as expected.

## Error 2: Terraform  - ‘ user_data ’ not working – SUDO

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-1.png" /></p>

After manually inputting ‘ sudo ’ on LINUX command within Ubuntu-VM

The NGINX installation script did not behave as expected when executed through EC2 startup configuration.

### Resolution

The Bash commands were explicitly configured with sudo :

```hcl
## SCRIPT --> to INSTALL & Configure NGNIX within server user_data = <<-EOF #!/ bin/bash sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get install nginx -y sudo systemctl enable nginx sudo systemctl start nginx EOF
```

## Error 3: Terraform  - ‘ user_data ’ not working – Script Format

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-16.png" /></p>

Upon checking ‘nginx’ service manually within VM

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-14.png" /></p>

After Executing:

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-11.png" /></p>

But simply adding “user_data_replace_on_change ” command won’t suffice.

### Problem

The project notes identified blank spaces around the EOF marker and possible issues with Terraform updating the startup script.

Still No Output: -

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-6.png" /></p>

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-2.png" /></p>

### Resolution

The EOF formatting was corrected (After removing SPACES inbetween within ‘EOF’), and user_data_replace_on_change was used:

```hcl
user_data = <<-EOF
```

#!/ bin/bash

sudo apt-get update -y

sudo apt-get install nginx -y

sudo  systemctl enable nginx

sudo  systemctl start nginx

EOF

user_data_replace_on_change = true ###Better Terraform solution: force replacement when user_data changes

### Result

The updated startup configuration worked.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-17.png" /></p>

# 🧠 Key Terraform Learning

### Terraform Lifecycle

The project notes introduce Terraform's lifecycle meta-argument.

```hcl
lifecycle {
```

create_before_destroy = true

}

This tells Terraform to create the replacement resource before destroying the existing resource when replacement is required.

### Concept

Without create_before_destroy :

Destroy old resource

↓

Create new resource

↓

Potential downtime

With create_before_destroy :

Create new resource

↓

Wait until ready

↓

Destroy old resource

↓

Reduced downtime

The notes also cover situations where create_before_destroy can be useful, such as load-balanced or production workloads, and why it may be unnecessary for a simple single-VM lab.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-13.png" /></p>

### prevent_destroy

The project notes also cover:

```hcl
lifecycle {
```

prevent_destroy = true

}

This prevents Terraform from destroying the protected resource.

Example use cases identified in the project notes include:

- Databases

- Critical EC2 instances

- Production storage

- Resources containing important data

This acts conceptually like a "DO NOT DELETE" protection mechanism.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-8.png" /></p>

### ignore_changes

Another lifecycle option covered is:

```hcl
lifecycle {
```

ignore_changes = [tags]

}

This can be useful when certain attributes are managed or modified outside Terraform.

The project notes specifically discuss tags and externally managed configuration as possible use cases.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-7.png" /></p>

# 🚀 Terraform `user_data`

The project uses EC2 user_data to automate initial server configuration.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-3.png" /></p>

Example:

```hcl
user_data = <<-EOF
```

#!/ bin/bash

sudo apt-get update -y

sudo apt-get install nginx -y

sudo  systemctl enable nginx

sudo  systemctl start nginx

EOF

### Why use user_data ?

Without startup automation, the administrator may need to log in to every new EC2 instance and repeat the configuration manually.

With user_data :

Terraform provisions EC2

↓

EC2 boots

↓

Startup script executes

↓

NGINX installed

↓

NGINX enabled

↓

NGINX started

This makes the deployment more repeatable and consistent.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-15.png" /></p>

# 🔄 `user_data` vs `user_data_replace_on_change`

The project notes highlight an important distinction.

### Default behavior

When user_data changes, Terraform normally performs a stop/start operation so the updated configuration can be applied.

user_data changed

↓

EC2 stopped

↓

EC2 started

### With user_data_replace_on_change = true

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-9.png" /></p>

user_data changed

↓

Existing EC2 destroyed

↓

New EC2 created

This should therefore be used carefully, particularly for production workloads where replacement could cause service disruption or data loss.

# 🔐 EC2 Key Pair / SSH Access

The project notes use an ED25519 key:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "terraform- ngnix -key-pair"
```

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-4.png" /></p>

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="screenshot-18.png" /></p>

The Terraform configuration references the public key:

```hcl
resource " aws_key_pair " " my_key " {
```

key_name = " tf -nginx-key"

public_key = file("~/.ssh/ ngnix_key_pair_repo /ngnix_key_pair.pub")

}

AWS's official EC2 documentation should be used for the current key-pair workflow.

For cleanup:

```bash
terraform destroy
```

If prevent_destroy = true is configured on a resource, Terraform will refuse to destroy that resource until the protection is intentionally removed or changed.
